title: Agitation and mixing
ends: Your batches will be well mixed.

steps.q: In turbulent flow, you double the agitator speed. What happens to the power draw?
steps.title: Power and speed
steps.summary: In turbulent flow, agitator power P = Np × ρ × N³ × D⁵, where Np is the power number, N the speed and D the impeller diameter. Doubling the speed raises power 2³ = 8 times; doubling the diameter at the same speed raises it 2⁵ = 32 times. Check motor current whenever agitator speed is changed.

steps.q: A tank with no baffles, agitator at high speed. What forms?
steps.title: Vortex
steps.summary: Without baffles the liquid rotates with the impeller like a solid body, giving poor top-to-bottom mixing, and the surface forms a vortex that can draw air or vapour into the batch. Wall baffles, usually four about one-tenth of the vessel diameter wide, break the rotation into axial flow. Glass-lined reactors have only one or two baffles and vortex more easily.

opts.t: A dead zone at the top

steps.q: You need to keep heavy solids off the bottom. Which impeller is the usual choice?
steps.title: Lift the solids
steps.summary: A pitched-blade turbine pumping down sends flow to the base, across the bottom and up the walls, lifting solids. Mount it low, about a quarter of the tank diameter off the base, to reach the corners. Radial disc turbines throw flow sideways and are better suited to gas dispersion than solids suspension.

steps.q: Scale up 10 times in diameter at the same power per volume. What happens to blend time?
steps.title: Scale-up
steps.summary: At constant power per volume, impeller speed scales with diameter to the power −2/3, and in turbulent flow blend time scales with 1/speed, so it grows with diameter to the power 2/3. Ten times the diameter gives about 4.6 times the blend time: a 10 s lab blend becomes about 46 s in the plant. Fast reactions may give more impurities on scale-up unless dosing is slower or into a better-mixed spot.

steps.q: A fast reaction where local excess makes impurities. Where should the reagent go in?
steps.title: Dosing point
steps.summary: For a fast reaction where local excess gives impurities, dose below the surface near the impeller, where turbulence spreads the reagent quickly. Dosing onto the surface near the wall leaves a rich patch in slow flow, giving side reactions a chance. Dose only with the agitator running and proven, fit the dip pipe with a siphon break so the batch cannot suck back, and dose slowly enough that each addition is mixed before the next arrives.

opts.t: On the surface near the wall
Below the surface, near the impeller

steps.q: Gas is fed through a ring sparger under the impeller. Which impeller handles the most gas?
board: Gas is fed through a ring
steps.title: Gas dispersion
steps.summary: With gas from a sparger under the impeller, a radial disc turbine handles the most gas: it throws gas and liquid outward through a high-shear zone, making small bubbles. Pitched-blade turbines flood at lower gas rates. If the gas rate is too high for the speed, the impeller floods, spinning in a gas pocket while gas rises straight through; large bubbles erupting around the shaft, with power falling further as gas increases, are the signs. Reduce gas, or raise speed if the motor has margin.

draw: fix: less gas, or more speed

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: agitators. Spinning metal that decides if your batch works. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Now scale up your own vessel in the mixing calculator.

q1.text: Question 1. In turbulent flow, you double the agitator speed. What happens to the power draw?

q1-r0.text: If only. Power climbs much faster than speed.

q1-r1.text: That's speed squared. Power goes one step further.

q1-r2.text: 8 times! Speed cubed. The motor feels every rpm.

q1-r3.text: The motor's ammeter would like a word.

q1-b0.text: In turbulent flow, power equals the power number, times density, times speed cubed, times diameter to the fifth.

q1-b1.text: Double the speed: two cubed is 8. Eight times the power.

q1-b2.text: Double the impeller diameter at the same speed: two to the fifth is 32. Thirty-two times the power.

q1-b3.text: So a small speed change can overload the motor or gearbox: 10 percent more speed is a third more power. Check the motor current when you change speed.

q2.text: Question 2. A tank with no baffles, agitator at high speed. What forms?

q2-r0.text: Vortex! The whole batch just spins like a washing machine.

q2-r1.text: Foam can follow later. First, think about rotation.

q2-r2.text: Nothing much? Run it without baffles and watch it swirl.

q2-r3.text: The trouble is the whole batch rotating, not just the top.

q2-b0.text: Without baffles, the liquid spins round with the impeller like a solid body. It looks busy, but little mixing happens.

q2-b1.text: The surface dips into a vortex. It can pull air or vapour down into the batch.

q2-b2.text: Baffles on the wall break the rotation and turn it into top-to-bottom flow. Usually four, about a tenth of the tank diameter wide.

q2-b3.text: Glass-lined reactors have only one or two baffles, so they vortex more easily. Keep that in mind at high speed.

q3.text: Question 3. You need to keep heavy solids off the bottom. Which impeller is the usual choice?

q3-r0.text: It throws flow sideways, not down to sweep the base.

q3-r1.text: Yes! Axial flow down, sweeping the bottom.

q3-r2.text: Anchors are for thick batches. In a thin liquid it just swirls, and solids pile up in the middle of the base.

q3-r3.text: A pump loop alone won't lift a heavy cake.

q3-b0.text: A pitched-blade turbine pumps liquid straight down to the base.

q3-b1.text: The flow sweeps across the bottom and up the walls, carrying the solids with it.

q3-b2.text: Place it low, about a quarter of the tank diameter off the bottom, so it reaches the corners.

q3-b3.text: Radial turbines throw flow sideways. They suit gas dispersion, not solids.

q4.text: Question 4. Scale up 10 times in diameter at the same power per volume. What happens to blend time?

q4-r0.text: That's ten to the one-third. The exponent is two-thirds.

q4-r1.text: Correct! Bigger tanks mix slower, even with the same P/V.

q4-r2.text: Too pessimistic. It's longer, but not in step with the diameter.

q4-r3.text: Same power per volume doesn't buy the same blend time.

q4-b0.text: Same power per volume means speed falls as the tank grows: speed goes with diameter to the minus two-thirds.

q4-b1.text: In turbulent flow, blend time goes with one over speed. So it grows with diameter to the two-thirds.

q4-b2.text: Ten times the diameter: ten to the two-thirds is about 4.6. A 10 second blend in the lab is about 46 seconds in the plant.

q4-b3.text: That's why a fast reaction that worked in the flask can give more impurities in the plant. Dose slower, or into a better-mixed spot.

q5.text: Question 5. A fast reaction where local excess makes impurities. Where should the reagent go in?

q5-r0.text: The wall is the sleepiest spot in the vessel. Worst choice.

q5-r1.text: Yes! Into the busiest spot, where it spreads fastest.

q5-r2.text: For a fast reaction, the first few seconds decide it.

q5-r3.text: From the manway? That's not dosing, that's hoping.

q5-b0.text: Near the wall at the surface, flow is slow. The reagent sits in a rich patch and reacts there.

q5-b1.text: A rich patch means local excess. Side reactions get their chance.

q5-b2.text: A dip pipe that ends near the impeller puts the reagent straight into the most turbulent zone.

q5-b3.text: Dose only with the agitator running, fit the dip pipe with a siphon break, and dose slowly enough that each drop is mixed before the next one arrives. Try your numbers in the mixing scale-up calculator on pharmacheme dot in.

q6.text: Question 6. Gas is fed through a ring sparger under the impeller. Which impeller handles the most gas?

q6-r0.text: Yes! The disc turbine chops the gas into fine bubbles.

q6-r1.text: It floods early with gas: the bubbles just pass through.

q6-r2.text: An anchor barely touches the gas. Bubbles stroll straight up.

q6-r3.text: Propellers are for blending thin liquids, not gas.

q6-b0.text: Gas rises from the sparger. The impeller has to break it into small bubbles and spread them out.

q6-b1.text: A radial disc turbine throws gas and liquid out to the wall in a strong shear zone. Small bubbles, big surface area.

q6-b2.text: Too much gas and the impeller floods: it spins in its own gas pocket and the gas goes straight up.

q6-b3.text: Power always dips when gas comes on. Flooding shows as big bubbles boiling up round the shaft, and power falling further as gas rises. Cut the gas, or raise the speed if the motor has margin.
